extracted.intended_audience: scientists, experimental philosophers, and students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying and judging the four classical inductive methods (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues) and related experimental design principles for establishing laws of causation in natural science. Emphasizes examples, limits, corroboration, and necessary controls for reliable induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive proof advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: This deductive proof ... has the advantage of at once proving causation as well as co-existence; and it has the additional advantage that it also accounts for the exceptions to the occurrence of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduction can simultaneously establish both causal relation and co-existence and explain exceptions that other methods might miss. Use deduction when properties of agents are known so that the effect follows necessarily from antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference (direct experiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second corroboration of the theory is by direct experiment, according to the canon of the Method of Difference. ... the difference in the muscular irritability was to be attributed [to the paralysis].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design paired or controlled comparisons that differ in only one material circumstance (A B C vs a b c). Repeat experiments sufficiently often in different subjects to exclude accidental/unrecognized differences. Use the Method of Difference to ascribe a difference in effect to a single differing antecedent; look for reversal when the antecedent is reversed (A B C → no consequent when antecedent removed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the canon, therefore, of the Method of Agreement, it may be inferred that there is a connection between the two facts. The Method of Agreement, indeed, as has been shown, is not competent to prove causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when many cases share only one common circumstance; infer that the common circumstance is the relevant antecedent. But be cautious: this method alone cannot establish causation — it indicates candidates for causal factors to be tested further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: On the principle, therefore, of the Method of Concomitant Variations, it may be inferred that the duration of the rigidity depends on the degree of the irritability; and that if the charge had been ... stronger ... the rigidity would have been shortened in a corresponding ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer causal relation when changes in the magnitude of an antecedent correspond proportionally to changes in the consequent. Useful to detect quantitative dependencies; corroborate by showing graded responses (more antecedent → more/less consequent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method (Agreement + Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: These are the conditions of the Joint Method of Agreement and Difference. ... The Joint Method, though really employed, has only a subordinate place in this particular investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine Agreement and Difference to isolate antecedents when cases agreeing and differing are available. Note limitation: like Agreement, Joint Method does not by itself prove causation unless causation of the aggregate antecedent is already established by other means (e.g., by Difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: It is by this process, in fact, that science, in its present advanced state, is chiefly promoted. ... when the effects of all known causes are estimated with exactness, and subducted, the residual facts are constantly appearing in the form of phenomena altogether new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate and subtract the effects of known causes from observed phenomena; treat the remainder (residue) as indicating additional causes or new phenomena. Requires accurate quantification of known causes where possible; residuals should be tested and may lead to discovery of new 'vera causae' (actually existing antecedents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural experiments as valid tests (nature performs controlled changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is observed that dew is never copiously deposited in situations much screened from the open sky, and not at all in a cloudy night; but if the clouds withdraw even for a few minutes, and leave a clear opening, a deposition of dew presently begins ... The proof, therefore, is complete, that the presence or absence of an uninterrupted communication with the sky causes the deposition or non-deposition of dew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When nature introduces a single, definite change and the effect follows rapidly (leaving no time for other material changes), this constitutes a valid test equivalent to an experimental Method of Difference. Use such natural experiments for corroboration when controlled manipulation is impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeatability and control to exclude accidental differences
rubrics_metrics.description: This assumption of complete resemblance in all material circumstances save one, evidently could not be safely made in any one pair of experiments ... but if ... the experiment was repeated sufficiently often in different animals to exclude the supposition that any abnormal circumstance could be present in them all, the conditions of the Method of Difference were adequately secured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on single paired comparisons; repeat across different subjects and conditions to rule out accidental or unobserved confounders. Ensure as far as possible that experimental units are alike in all material respects except the factor under test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by multiple independent methods
rubrics_metrics.description: This deductive proof ... the second corroboration ... by direct experiment ... and, finally, even on that great scale we are able to verify the result. ... The proof, therefore, is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strengthen inferences by assembling different kinds of evidence (deduction from known properties, direct experiment, and natural observation). Converging lines of evidence reduce the chance that an induction is accidental or spurious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to calculate and subtract known causes for Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: To have made it exemplify the Method of Residues, the effect of the resistance of the air and that of the rigidity of the silk should have been calculated a priori, from the laws obtained by separate and foregone experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a true residue analysis, known causal contributions should be quantified a priori (when possible) based on prior laws/experiments; only after subtracting these should one treat the remainder as a residual phenomenon meriting further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the Four Methods and necessity of reduction to comparable elements
rubrics_metrics.description: He objects that they take for granted the very thing which is most difficult to discover, the reduction of the phenomena to formulæ such as are here presented... The greatest difficulty ... is, first, that of obtaining the evidence, and next, of reducing it to the form which tests its conclusiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that applying these methods presumes the investigator can identify candidate antecedent elements (A, B, C, etc.). The methods are tools to test inductions once the relevant elements are posited; they do not automatically yield the decomposition. Use the methods to judge inductive arguments, but accept that formulating hypotheses remains a hard creative task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat on overclaiming causation from Agreement/Joint Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The defect of that Method is, that like the Method of Agreement ... it can not prove causation. ... It being, therefore, beyond doubt that the aggregate antecedent, the death, is the actual cause of the whole train of consequents, whatever of the circumstances attending the death can be shown to be followed in all its variations by variations in the effect under investigation, must be the particular feature of the fact of death on which that effect depends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer causation solely from Agreement or Joint methods unless additional proof (e.g., from Difference) establishes that the aggregate antecedent is causal. Use these methods to identify candidate causal features, then test them by Difference or other means that can establish causation.
